articles.title: Cientistas criam exército de polvos devoradores de caranguejos | G1
articles.standfirst: Na Itália, o caranguejo-azul, originário do Atlântico, vem causando prejuízos milionários. Cientistas agora tentam reduzir população do crustáceo, que virou uma praga.
articles.summary: Na Itália, o caranguejo-azul, originário do Atlântico, vem causando prejuízos milionários. Cientistas agora tentam reduzir população do crustáceo, que virou uma praga.
articles.body:
Polvo-comum (Octopus vulgaris) escondido em uma fenda no Mar Mediterrâneo, perto de Plakias, na ilha de Creta, na Grécia. — Foto: Martijn Klijnstra/Wikimedia Commons

No Mar Adriático, cientistas na Itália estão soltando milhares de filhotes de polvo a partir de um barco pesqueiro na tentativa de conter uma espécie invasora de caranguejo que vem causando grandes prejuízos à pesca local.

Uma equipe da Universidade de Bolonha aposta que o polvo-comum pode ajudar a conter o avanço da população de caranguejos-azuis, um crustáceo voraz que tem devastado a produção de mariscos no Adriático.

"Escolhemos o polvo porque, em seu habitat natural, ele é um predador extremamente eficiente de crustáceos", afirmou à AFP Antonio Casalini, um dos pesquisadores.

Originário da costa do Atlântico na América do Norte, o caranguejo-azul chegou ao Mediterrâneo há décadas, provavelmente transportado pela água de lastro dos navios, que é captada para garantir a estabilidade das embarcações.

No entanto, a população do crustáceo aumentou drasticamente nos últimos anos, e tanto o governo quanto as associações de pescadores atribuem essa explosão populacional ao aquecimento das águas e às mudanças climáticas.

Com pinças afiadas e de tom azulado, especialmente eficazes para abrir conchas, os caranguejos-azuis têm causado grandes estragos no nordeste da Itália, uma das principais regiões produtoras de moluscos da Europa.

No ano passado, as autoridades da Emilia-Romagna, região cuja capital é Bolonha, informaram que a espécie havia causado prejuízos de quase 17 milhões de euros (R$ 102 milhões) desde 2022.

A Coldiretti, principal organização agrícola e pesqueira da Itália, estima que as perdas cheguem a cerca de 200 milhões de euros (R$ 1,2 bilhão) em todo o país. A região do Vêneto, no norte italiano, também foi severamente afetada.

"Ele come de tudo, inclusive as jovens amêijoas que vivem no fundo do mar", explica Davide Sanulli, pescador e produtor de mexilhões de 64 anos. Nas áreas de lagoas próximas ao delta do rio Pó, o caranguejo-azul provocou uma "verdadeira devastação", acrescentou Sanulli, que colabora com o projeto da Universidade de Bolonha.

Excelentes nadadores e capazes de atingir até um quilo, esses caranguejos têm poucos predadores naturais. É essa realidade que os pesquisadores querem mudar.

Lançado no ano passado e financiado pelo governo da região de Emilia-Romanha, o projeto Octo-Blu busca aumentar a população de polvos para conter o avanço desses invasores de carapaça dura.

A equipe cria polvos recém-nascidos em tanques de água instalados em um laboratório na cidade portuária de Cesenatico.

Quando estão prontos, os pequenos invertebrados são recolhidos aos milhares em grandes sacos plásticos e levados para o mar, às vezes a bordo do robusto barco pesqueiro azul de Davide Sanulli.

Em seguida, os filhotes são soltos próximos a recifes submarinos, onde o grupo instalou abrigos artificiais de cimento e argila para aumentar as chances de sobrevivência dos polvos.

Desde junho, dezenas de milhares de exemplares já foram liberados. A AFP informou inicialmente que cerca de 80 mil polvos haviam sido soltos, enquanto a revista Scientific American elevou posteriormente essa estimativa para aproximadamente 130 mil.

A equipe do Octo-Blu espera dobrar esse número até o fim de agosto, na expectativa de que parte dos animais sobreviva até a fase adulta.

"A ideia é formar uma pequena comunidade próxima à costa para que ela possa ajudar a conter com mais eficiência a expansão do caranguejo-azul", afirmou Casalini, técnico em aquicultura.

Caranguejo azul pesca em cenote mexicano. — Foto: Martin Broen

O projeto tem algumas limitações evidentes. O polvo-comum normalmente não vive nas águas quentes e arenosas típicas das áreas lagunares onde o caranguejo-azul tem causado os maiores estragos. Por isso, seu impacto nessas regiões provavelmente seria limitado, algo de que os próprios pesquisadores estão cientes.

Outros especialistas sugerem que o robalo poderia ser mais eficaz no controle do caranguejo. Enquanto isso, a equipe da Universidade de Bolonha também estuda o uso de enguias, grandes consumidoras de ovos de crustáceos, como complemento à ação dos polvos.

Ainda assim, caso o projeto-piloto seja ampliado, ele poderá ajudar a reduzir a população do caranguejo-azul e os impactos que a espécie vem causando ao ecossistema marinho da costa do Adriático, afirma Casalini.

"Os caranguejos-azuis têm um potencial reprodutivo e uma taxa de fertilidade impressionantes", explica Pietro Emmanuele, também pesquisador da Universidade de Bolonha. Segundo ele, uma única fêmea pode colocar milhões de ovos, e a maior parte deles chega a eclodir em filhotes.

Embora apenas uma fração das crias sobreviva até a idade adulta, a captura de uma única fêmea por um polvo já poderia fazer diferença no controle da população da espécie, destacou o pesquisador.

articles.title: Cardiologia mundial: só exame de sangue alterado não fecha diagnóstico | G1
articles.standfirst: Consenso internacional troca a antiga divisão em cinco tipos por três categorias baseadas no que causou a lesão e detalha como sintomas, eletrocardiograma, imagem e marcadores no sangue precisam ser lidos em conjunto.
articles.summary: Consenso internacional troca a antiga divisão em cinco tipos por três categorias baseadas no que causou a lesão; sintomas, eletrocardiograma, imagem e mais devem ser lidos juntos.
articles.body:
Internações de pacientes com até 39 anos por infarto mais que dobraram nos últimos 15 anos — Foto: Reprodução/TV TEM

Um mesmo resultado de troponina alta no sangue pode significar um infarto —ou uma entre mais de uma dezena de outras condições que nada têm a ver com entupimento de artéria. É em torno dessa distinção que as principais sociedades de cardiologia do mundo reorganizaram a forma de definir e classificar o infarto do miocárdio.

A mudança está na 5ª Definição Universal de Infarto do Miocárdio , publicada nesta sexta-feira (28) no periódico European Heart Journal. O documento aposenta a classificação que separava os casos em tipos 1, 2, 3, 4 e 5 e passa a agrupá-los conforme o mecanismo que desencadeou a lesão no coração .

Foi elaborado em conjunto pela Sociedade Europeia de Cardiologia (ESC), pelo American College of Cardiology (ACC), pela American Heart Association (AHA) e pela World Heart Federation (WHF), com especialistas de 12 países e cinco continentes.

Os casos passam a ser distribuídos em três grandes grupos, definidos pela origem do problema. O infarto primário nasce em uma alteração aguda da própria artéria coronária. O secundário aparece quando outra doença desequilibra a relação entre o oxigênio que chega ao coração e o de que ele precisa. E o relacionado a procedimento surge como complicação de uma intervenção cardíaca.

Antes, cada infarto ganhava um número conforme o mecanismo e o contexto do evento, mas algumas dessas gavetas juntavam situações muito diferentes. O antigo tipo 2 abrigava tanto problemas agudos da própria coronária —como dissecção, embolia ou vasoespasmo— quanto quadros em que outra doença fazia o coração receber menos oxigênio do que precisava.

Para os autores, era uma estrutura difícil de aplicar do mesmo modo em toda parte e que nem sempre revelava o mecanismo por trás do evento. Amarrar a classificação à origem do infarto, resume o cirurgião cardiovascular Ricardo Kazunori, da BP - A Beneficência Portuguesa de São Paulo, é o avanço mais direto da revisão.

Infarto primário: o problema começa na artéria

O infarto primário se dá quando há uma alteração aguda na circulação coronariana —o conjunto de artérias que leva sangue ao músculo do coração. A causa mais comum continua sendo a aterotrombose: uma placa de aterosclerose na parede do vaso se rompe ou sofre erosão, favorece a formação de um coágulo e esse coágulo reduz ou interrompe o fluxo de sangue.

Agora a categoria reúne também outros mecanismos agudos das coronárias, como a dissecção espontânea da artéria, a embolia, o vasoespasmo, a reestenose ou trombose de stent em certas situações e a falha de enxerto quando ocorre mais de 30 dias após a revascularização.

O ponto em comum, explica Kazunori, é a origem: todos partem de uma alteração aguda da própria coronária. Identificar qual deles está em jogo continua decisivo, porque mecanismos distintos podem pedir investigação e tratamento diferentes —daí o peso que a definição dá à angiografia coronariana e a exames capazes de mostrar o que aconteceu dentro do vaso.

Infarto secundário: outra doença sufoca o coração

No infarto secundário, não é preciso haver uma obstrução aguda da artéria por um coágulo. O que ocorre é um descompasso: outra condição faz o oxigênio que chega ao coração ficar aquém do que o órgão precisa naquele momento.

A oferta pode cair —numa anemia importante, numa baixa oxigenação do sangue ou numa pressão muito baixa— ou a demanda pode disparar, como em certas taquicardias e na hipertensão intensa.Kazunori cita a hemoglobina muito baixa de uma anemia grave, ou uma hipoxemia, como exemplos de oxigênio insuficiente chegando ao músculo.

Elzo Mattar, diretor do Departamento de Hipertensão Arterial da Sociedade Brasileira de Cardiologia (SBC) e professor da Faculdade Estadual de Medicina de São José do Rio Preto (Famerp), lembra dos quadros mais graves, como o choque séptico, em que o infarto surge como desdobramento de outra doença.

É nessa categoria que a nova definição aperta o critério. Ter uma doença capaz de gerar o desequilíbrio e apresentar troponina alta não basta: é preciso reunir evidência de que houve isquemia e lesão do músculo cardíaco compatíveis com um infarto —o que ajuda a separar quem de fato infartou de quem tem uma lesão no coração provocada por outro processo.

Para onde correr se achar que está tendo um infarto? — Foto: Getty Images

Complicações de cateter e cirurgia sob mesmo guarda-chuva

O terceiro grupo reúne os infartos ligados a procedimentos cardíacos, como intervenções por cateter e cirurgias, em que o evento decorre de uma complicação que compromete a circulação do coração. Antes, procedimentos percutâneos e cirurgia de revascularização tinham categorias separadas, com critérios que exigiam troponina cinco ou dez vezes acima do limite de referência.

A nova proposta uniformiza esses diagnósticos, abandona os múltiplos do marcador como base principal e passa a considerar complicações do procedimento dentro de uma janela de até 30 dias, com critérios objetivos de imagem e de lesão do músculo.

Kazunori ilustra: a pessoa que vai colocar um stent e sofre uma complicação que fecha uma artéria, ou quem faz uma cirurgia de revascularização e tem um problema numa anastomose que leva ao infarto. A ideia é distinguir uma variação nos marcadores, comum depois de qualquer intervenção, de um infarto realmente provocado por uma complicação relevante.

A revisão não só cria grupos: também apaga uma categoria. O infarto tipo 3 nomeava a morte cardíaca em que o infarto era a causa provável, mas o paciente morria antes que os exames de confirmação pudessem ser feitos.

Esses casos passam a ser enquadrados como primários, secundários ou relacionados a procedimento, conforme o contexto clínico ou os achados de autópsia, quando houver.

Exame de sangue não diz sozinho qual foi a causa

A troponina está no centro dessa investigação porque funciona como um marcador de lesão das células cardíacas —uma proteína do músculo do coração que escapa para a corrente sanguínea quando essas células se lesionam. Pela nova definição, existe lesão miocárdica aguda quando seus níveis sobem e/ou caem ao longo das medições e ao menos um resultado ultrapassa o percentil 99 fixado como limite de referência do exame.

Isso, por si, não equivale a um infarto. A troponina também sobe em situações como miocardite, sepse, insuficiência cardíaca aguda, embolia pulmonar, hipertensão grave, síndrome de Takotsubo, AVC, crises epilépticas, exercício físico intenso e alguns tratamentos contra o câncer.

A fronteira, resume Kazunori, está na isquemia: se o marcador sobe e há critérios de isquemia, cabe falar em infarto; se sobe sem esses critérios, é preciso procurar outra causa. Para confirmar o diagnóstico, o médico avalia o quadro inteiro —além da troponina, pesam sintomas compatíveis, alterações novas no eletrocardiograma e exames de imagem—, e o próprio consenso reconhece que nenhum critério isolado dá conta de todos os casos.

Há ainda um cenário em que a troponina permanece alta sem lesão nova: a lesão miocárdica crônica, quando o marcador fica persistentemente elevado num paciente estável, por doenças cardíacas crônicas ou outras alterações na estrutura do coração.

A função dos rins entra nessa leitura, já que a menor capacidade de eliminar a troponina da circulação pode manter os níveis altos. Por isso, muitas vezes não importa só quanto o exame marca, mas como esse valor se comporta ao longo do tempo e conversa com os demais achados.

Mulheres passam a ter valores de referência próprios

A nova definição reforça o uso de limites de troponina específicos para cada sexo. O percentil 99 de referência costuma ser mais baixo entre mulheres, e aplicar um único ponto de corte aos dois sexos abre espaço para que lesões cardíacas —infartos inclusive— deixem de ser reconhecidas em algumas pacientes.

Adotar valores por sexo, segundo o consenso, reduz esse viés e o risco de subdiagnóstico feminino. A diferença não é só laboratorial, observa Kazunori: o ponto de corte adotado é o que define quais pacientes seguem para investigação adicional e quais são liberados.

MINOCA vira ponto de partida, não conclusão

Outro conceito revisto é o MINOCA , sigla aplicada a pacientes com lesão cardíaca e coronárias sem obstrução importante.

A 5ª definição passa a tratá-lo como "lesão miocárdica com artérias coronárias não obstrutivas" e, mais do que isso, como um diagnóstico de trabalho —uma etapa, não o fim da linha. Encontrar troponina alta sem obstrução significativa não encerra a busca pela causa; é, nas palavras de Kazunori, um cenário que leva a investigação a outro nível.

Exames como a ressonância magnética cardíaca e métodos mais detalhados de avaliação das coronárias ajudam a separar um problema coronariano de outras doenças capazes de agredir o músculo.

Os números de mulheres brasileiras de 18 a 49 anos vítimas de infarto aumentaram na última década — Foto: GETTY IMAGES

Os exames de imagem assumem um papel maior tanto para confirmar o infarto quanto para identificar seu mecanismo. A angiografia coronariana invasiva segue como referência para avaliar as coronárias em pacientes selecionados e pode revelar não só a obstrução, mas qual alteração aguda está por trás dela; conforme o caso, ecocardiograma, tomografia das coronárias e ressonância magnética cardíaca também entram.

Reunir essas informações, e não olhar apenas para a troponina, é o que fecha o diagnóstico, diz Kazunori —algo especialmente útil nos casos menos típicos, em que sintomas e eletrocardiograma não dão resposta clara.

Um diagnóstico possível onde faltam exames

O documento dedica atenção especial aos serviços de saúde sem acesso a exames laboratoriais e a métodos avançados de imagem, ponto que Mattar faz questão de destacar.

O pano de fundo é um contraste: em 2021, o mundo registrou 31,9 milhões de novos casos de doença isquêmica do coração, 31,8% a mais do que em 2010, enquanto o acesso aos recursos para diagnosticar um infarto segue desigual. Um estudo citado no consenso mostrou que, em Uganda, apenas 43% dos serviços avaliados tinham dosagem de troponina e 55% dispunham de eletrocardiograma.

Para esses lugares, a diretriz fixa critérios próprios: o diagnóstico pode ser presumido quando o paciente tem sintomas compatíveis com isquemia somados a alterações características no eletrocardiograma, como novas mudanças isquêmicas ou o surgimento de ondas Q patológicas.

Sem troponina nem imagem aprofundada, explica Mattar, o médico se apoia na clínica, no tipo de dor e no eletrocardiograma —e autorizar esse diagnóstico presumido ajuda o profissional de uma região carente a agir a tempo, evitando que alguém em pleno infarto seja liberado sem tratamento.

O consenso menciona, ainda, a telemedicina na leitura de eletrocardiogramas e a expansão dos testes de troponina no próprio ponto de atendimento.

Por que a mudança pode mexer nas estatísticas

Classificar um infarto não interfere apenas na ficha do paciente: é essa etiqueta que define como os casos entram nas bases de internação e mortalidade, como estudos clínicos selecionam participantes e como países comparam resultados.

A contabilidade, porém, emperra: a expansão dos testes de troponina de alta sensibilidade e a definição anterior elevaram em 11% os diagnósticos do antigo tipo 1 e em 22% os do tipo 2, mas, em dois países europeus, menos de 20% dos pacientes que preenchiam os critérios da antiga definição para o tipo 2 chegaram a receber um código de infarto na CID-10.

Para estreitar essa distância, a nova classificação foi construída com a Organização Mundial da Saúde e propõe códigos da CID-11 capazes de diferenciar os infartos primários, secundários e relacionados a procedimentos, além de separar os eventos com e sem elevação do segmento ST no eletrocardiograma.

Ao reduzir as categorias e prendê-las ao mecanismo que causou a lesão, os autores esperam aproximar o que o médico encontra no atendimento do que é registrado nas estatísticas e estudado nas pesquisas.

articles.title: Parque Madureira recebe festival gospel Canto Pela Paz | G1
articles.standfirst: Festival de música gospel reúne artistas nacionais e ações de conscientização social. Evento é gratuito e começa às 16h.
articles.summary: Festival de música gospel reúne artistas nacionais e ações de conscientização social. Evento é gratuito e começa às 16h.
articles.body:
O Parque Madureira, na Zona Norte do Rio, recebe neste sábado (29) a terceira edição do Canto Pela Paz, festival de música gospel que reúne artistas nacionais e ações de conscientização social. O evento começa às 16h, tem entrada gratuita e classificação livre.

A programação faz parte das comemorações pelos 15 anos do Canto Pela Paz, criado em 2010, em São Paulo. No Rio, o festival chega à terceira edição com shows de Fernanda Brum, Samuel Messias, Lukas Agustinho, Arthur Calazans, Samuel Miranda, Alex Lúcio, Na Graça, Téo Brasil, DJ Prince e Allison e Vitória.

Além das apresentações musicais, o evento promove ações de conscientização sobre a importância da doação de sangue. Segundo a organização, desde a criação do projeto, milhares de pessoas já participaram das iniciativas, que também resultaram na distribuição gratuita de mais de 2 milhões de livros do pastor Juanribe Pagliarin, da Comunidade Cristã Paz e Vida.

O público também poderá acompanhar uma ilustração ao vivo apresentada pelo pastor Juanribe Pagliarin. A organização informou que uma história inédita, preparada especialmente para o público carioca, será apresentada durante o evento.

Com patrocínio da Prefeitura do Rio, o evento é aberto ao público e deve reunir famílias, integrantes de igrejas e frequentadores do Parque Madureira.

Line-up: Fernanda Brum, Samuel Messias, Lukas Agustinho, Arthur Calazans, Samuel Miranda, Alex Lúcio, Na Graça, Téo Brasil, DJ Prince e Allison e Vitória.

articles.title: 'I still struggle': Landlady recalls Saudi man who brought 9/11 hijackers to her office
articles.summary: US News: Holly Ratchford, who managed a residential complex in California's San Diego where two of the 9/11 hijackers lived, has spoken publicly for the first .
articles.body: Holly Ratchford, who managed a residential complex in California's San Diego where two of the 9/11 hijackers lived, has spoken publicly for the first time about her encounters with Saudi national Omar al-Bayoumi, who is accused of helping the two men before the attacks.Speaking to the BBC, Ratchford said she still struggles to reconcile the friendly man she knew with the allegations surrounding him. “It's almost impossible for me to wrap my head around who he said he was, and who he really is. I still struggle with that,” she said.Bayoumi moved with his family into Parkwood Apartments in September 1999 and soon became a regular at Ratchford's pool parties. She described him as “always so bubbly and smiling” and “very, very friendly”.In February 2000, Bayoumi brought two men, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar, to Ratchford's office seeking an apartment. The pair did not meet the complex's income requirements, but Bayoumi co-signed their lease and helped them open a bank account.Hazmi and Mihdhar later became two of the 19 al-Qaeda members who hijacked four US passenger planes on September 11, 2001.The two were on American Airlines Flight 77, which crashed into the Pentagon.Ratchford said she had no reason at the time to suspect the men. “There was absolutely nothing unusual about them. They were nice, they were polite,” she told the BBC.She later learned of their identities in the aftermath of the attacks, when a woman who claimed to be seeking a rental reference asked her whether she knew they were terrorists who had flown a plane into the Pentagon.“And I went, ‘What?’” Ratchford recalled.The FBI interviewed her on September 14, 2001, and obtained Bayoumi's guarantor form. Former FBI investigator Richard Lambert told the BBC that investigators later identified “a network headed up by Omar al-Bayoumi”.Bayoumi has long faced allegations that he facilitated the hijackers' activities in San Diego.In an August 2025 ruling, a New York federal judge found that evidence created a “reasonable inference” that Bayoumi and a Saudi diplomat had been coordinating with the Saudi government while assisting the hijackers. Saudi Arabia and Bayoumi have denied the allegations and Saudi Arabia is appealing the ruling.Ratchford, who has provided a sealed declaration to the New York court, said she has been haunted by her connection to the three men for the past 25 years.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: TCS techie on way home dies after reversing JCB rams his bike in Gurgaon
articles.summary: GURGAON: A 27-year-old systems engineer with Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Tushar Kumar, was killed late Thursday night after a reversing earthmove.
articles.body: GURGAON: A 27-year-old systems engineer with Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Tushar Kumar, was killed late Thursday night after a reversing earthmover engaged in road work rammed into his motorcycle near Moulsari Avenue Rapid Metro station.The machine’s driver fled the spot.Tushar was returning home from work around 11.30pm when his Royal Enfield was hit by the JCB earthmover’s rear bucket.The impact threw him and the bike onto the road. He was rushed to Narayana Hospital in DLF Phase 3, where doctors declared him dead. He was wearing a helmet at the time of the accident.Sources said GMDA was carrying out routine maintenance work at the site.Tushar had been working in the city for four years and was staying with his uncle in Ramprastha City, Sector 37D, while his parents lived in Mathura. He was their only child.Police said a passerby informed them about the incident around 11.45pm.“He usually left work around the same time every day. He had bought the bike about a year ago and would use it to travel to and from work. We never imagined that one day he would leave for work and not return,” said his father, Harish Kumar.Harish said police informed him of the accident, and he reached the hospital around 3.30am, where he identified his son’s body at the mortuary.“I reached the hospital and saw my son there. He was our only child. We had sent him to Gurgaon to work and build his future,” he said.In his complaint, Harish alleged that the work was being carried out at night in the middle of the road without proper directions or indicators. Police said they are examining this allegation.A police officer said that on receiving information from the hospital, a team reached the spot and found the JCB, bearing registration number HR-36-AN-7050, abandoned. articles.title: 'Like a movie scene': Chain of events that led to Nepal floods that killed over 600
articles.summary: South Asia News: A massive glacier and rock collapse high in Nepal’s Himalayas appears to have set off a chain of events that culminated in one of the country’s deadli.
articles.body: A massive glacier and rock collapse high in Nepal’s Himalayas appears to have set off a chain of events that culminated in one of the country’s deadliest flash floods in years, killing over 600 people and leaving thousands missing in Nepal and neighbouring Tibet.The disaster began high in the mountains on Wednesday when a huge section of glacier and rock collapsed into the Lhende Khola valley near the Nepal-China border. The falling mass blocked the river before a surge of water, ice and debris burst through the valley, sweeping downstream into the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems.The scale of the destruction has since become clearer. Bodies have been recovered hundreds of kilometres downstream in Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahun and both East and West Nawalparasi, according to Nepal Police, tracing the path of the flood through the country's major river systems.From glacier collapse to a wall of waterInitial reports suggested that an earthquake may have triggered an avalanche and blocked the Lhende Khola, creating a temporary dam that later burst. The US Geological Survey initially linked the flooding to a magnitude 4.4 earthquake recorded in the area.Satellite imagery, however, offered a different explanation. Images analysed after the disaster showed that a section of glacier and underlying rock, roughly 600 metres (2,000 feet) wide, had collapsed from an altitude of about 5,200 metres. The mass plunged around 1,200 metres into the valley below.The USGS later revised its assessment, concluding that the collapse itself produced a seismic signal equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake.Scientists cited in earlier reports said the enormous amount of ice stored at such a height would have carried immense potential energy as it fell. The impact pulverised ice and rock, sending a mixture of water and debris towards the Lhende Khola and then into the Bhotekoshi River.Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology reached a similar conclusion after examining satellite imagery provided by China. Binod Parajuli, a senior divisional hydrologist, said the evidence pointed to a combination of an ice avalanche, permafrost movement and a rockslide."The avalanche originated on Nepali territory, but after it came down it crossed the Nepal-China border, causing extensive damage on both sides," Parajuli told The Kathmandu Post.The exact sequence and contribution of each factor are still being assessed.Flood races downstream as new lake raises fresh fearsThe initial surge flattened settlements, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure on both sides of the border. In Nepal's Rasuwa district, soldiers were deployed to rescue people trapped inside a tunnel at the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, where thick mud made it difficult to locate the entrances and exits.By early Saturday, Nepal's disaster-management authority had reported 626 deaths, while Nepal Police put the toll at 553. More than 3,700 people had been rescued and 1,924 remained unaccounted for. China reported seven deaths and 554 missing.The disaster also created a new danger. A lake formed upstream after the glacier collapse and began overflowing, prompting warnings that another surge could hit communities downstream. Rescue teams were temporarily ordered to stop advancing while authorities assessed the threat. Chinese monitoring data later showed the lake's water level had fallen by about 10 metres from its peak.The disaster has also raised wider concerns about a rapidly warming Himalaya, where glaciers are retreating and mountain communities face increasing risks from landslides, glacial floods and unstable permafrost.For survivors, however, the disaster unfolded in seconds. Karbir Gaire, a customs officer in the border village of Timure, told reporters that he felt the ground shake before seeing what he described as a "black storm" racing towards the settlement.He and others ran uphill, escaping moments before the torrent struck."It was like a Hollywood movie scene," Gaire told news agency AP. "I don't call it a flood. It was a tsunami."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A former Illinois elementary school closed in 2014; its site has now become a $1.35 million fully accessible park with an inclusive playground, walking paths and a new splash pad
articles.summary: US News: On August 26 at 11:30, roughly 75 people gathered at Cooke Park for the official ribbon-cutting, capping a years-long transformation of the former Coo.
articles.body: On August 26 at 11:30, roughly 75 people gathered at Cooke Park for the official ribbon-cutting, capping a years-long transformation of the former Cooke Elementary School property into a fully accessible neighbourhood park. The ceremony, conducted by the Galesburg Area Chamber of Commerce, took place with the new splash pad running behind the crowd, water spraying and a light mist drifting over the gathering. The $1.352 million project includes an inclusive playground, a picnic shelter, restrooms, a bicycle repair station, walking paths and a parking area, along with the splash pad that was completed this month, according to WGIL.com.In attendance were state legislators, Mayor Peter Schwartzman, four City Council members, city officials and members of the public. Among those giving remarks were Mayor Schwartzman, Ward 4 Alderman Dwight White, whose ward includes the park, State Senator Mike Halpin, State Representative Dan Swanson, and Director of Parks and Recreation Don Miles. Several people who helped lead the push for the park also spoke, including Gayla Pacheco, Karen Ford-Kelley and Stephanie Jackson Grimes. Schwartzman, who has served as mayor for a little over five years, called the ceremony one of the proudest moments of his time in office.“This is a testament to good government, when all different levels of government, from state to local, and then the local community, work together and partner on a project that will have meaning not only immediately, but in the distant future,” Schwartzman said. "There are hundreds of people who played a role in making this happen. I thank you all, and may this park last another hundred years," he added.A former schoolFor several people at Wednesday's ceremony, the site carried much more significance and history. Cooke Elementary School operated on the property for decades before closing in 2014, and a handful of attendees who grew up nearby shared memories from their own school days there.White attended Cooke School from second through sixth grade. He said he still carries a scar from his time on the playground. “I scarred my leg over here chasing a boy ’cause I liked the girl,” White said. “It’s just so many great memories. Baseball out here, I tried out for Little League over here. It was just a place for the community.”White said he hopes the new park will do for the whole city what the old school grounds once did for his neighbourhood. “There’ll be some people over here that came from the north side of town, and they’re gonna meet some kid from the south side of town, and they don’t know where they’re from, and they’re gonna become friends,” White said. “That’s what this is gonna do, I hope.”Margaret Gimenez, who attended Cooke School in the 1940s, said she and a friend, Darlene Howard, were the first girls to serve as patrol guards at the school after she asked the principal why only boys held the role. “I said, ‘How come you don’t have girl patrol boys?'” Gimenez said. “She says, ‘You want to be one?’ I said, ‘Yeah.'”Gimenez said the school grounds had none of the equipment found at the new park. “We didn’t have swings or nothing. We had a monkey bar,” Gimenez said. “I’m so happy that (Pacheco) took the initiative to do this, and I know it was hard work. I’m proud of her.”The city purchased the former school property in December 2022 to create a neighbourhood park that is accessible, inclusive and welcoming to all residents. The site was chosen after strong public support for more recreational amenities on Galesburg’s southwest side.A new playgroundPacheco, a Galesburg native who grew up near the school, is widely credited with spearheading the push to build the park. She said the idea grew out of conversations during the Heart & Soul community planning process around 2021 and 2022.“The thing that people were asking for was free things to do,” Pacheco said. She began working with the city around 2022 to explore turning the vacant site into a park, using a $500,000 Open Space Land Acquisition and Development grant, administered by the Illinois Department of Natural Resources (IDNR), matched by the City of Galesburg. The addition of the splash pad was made possible through a $250,000 Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity (DCEO) grant secured with support from State Senator Mike Halpin and private donations raised by the citizen-led Cooke Park Project group.Pacheco said her favourite feature is the new splash pad. “I really love those butterflies,” she said. “It reminds me of art.” Reflecting on the years of work behind the project, Pacheco credited the people around her. “It takes a village,” Pacheco said. “If you have really good family and friends, I think you can get anything done.”“We are extremely grateful to the State of Illinois, IDNR, Senator Halpin and the dedicated members of the Cooke Park project group whose advocacy and fundraising brought this project to life,” said Eric Hanson, City Manager. “Seeing children and families already enjoying the playground—and now the new splash pad—is a testament to what our community can achieve together.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A New Orleans couple found a 2,000-year-old Roman tombstone in their backyard; the FBI traced it to Italy and returned it 80 years later
articles.summary: US News: In early 2025, Daniella Santoro, an anthropologist at Tulane University, and her partner, Aaron Lorenz, were clearing weeds behind their home in New O.
articles.body: In early 2025, Daniella Santoro, an anthropologist at Tulane University, and her partner, Aaron Lorenz, were clearing weeds behind their home in New Orleans' historic Carrollton neighbourhood when they uncovered a marble slab covered in Latin writing. Santoro contacted D. Ryan Gray, an archaeologist at the University of New Orleans, who shared photographs of the stone with Harald Stadler, an archaeologist at the University of Innsbruck, and Susann Lusnia, a classical archaeologist at Tulane. Lusnia recognised the inscription as an ancient Roman funerary monument. The stone commemorated Sextus Congenius Verus, a 42-year-old sailor who had served for 22 years aboard a ship called the Asclepius. Further research established that the marble monument had once belonged to the collection of the National Archaeological Museum in Civitavecchia, Italy, where it had eventually been recorded as missing. Its discovery transformed an unremarkable garden stone into a nearly 2,000-year-old artefact with a traceable history.How researchers identified the missing Roman tombstoneAccording to the FBI's New Orleans field office, the inscription and physical characteristics of the marble allowed researchers to connect the New Orleans discovery with a funerary monument missing from the National Archaeological Museum in Civitavecchia. The museum is located in the Italian coastal city of Civitavecchia, northwest of Rome. Once the identification was established, Santoro and the researchers worked with authorities to return the artefact to Italy. The FBI's Art Crime Team became involved in the repatriation process. Researchers initially considered whether the monument might have disappeared during the upheaval surrounding World War II. Civitavecchia was heavily damaged by Allied bombing during the war, creating the possibility that objects from the museum's collection could have been displaced during the destruction. The circumstances of the stone's disappearance, however, remained uncertain, and the eventual discovery in Louisiana provided a much clearer trail than researchers had previously had.How a family connection revealed how the Roman stone reached New OrleansThe breakthrough came after news of the discovery became public. Erin Scott O'Brien, who had previously lived at the New Orleans property, learned about the Roman monument and immediately recognised the stone from her family's history. The artefact had belonged to her grandparents. Her grandfather, Charles Paddock, had served in Italy during World War II, and the stone eventually made its way into the family's possession. O'Brien did not know that it was an ancient Roman funerary monument. In 2004, she placed the stone in the garden of the New Orleans property. She later explained that the family had planted a tree and decided to put the unusual stone outside in the garden as part of the new home's landscaping. For years, the monument remained there without anyone realising what it was. It was only after Santoro and Lorenz uncovered it beneath the vegetation and archaeologists examined the inscription that its true age and history came to light. The family has not established exactly how Paddock acquired the monument in Italy. It remains possible that he purchased it, obtained it through another transaction or brought it home as a wartime souvenir, but there is no definitive family record explaining how it left Italy.What Sextus Congenius Verus's gravestone tells us about Roman lifeThe inscription provides a remarkably specific glimpse into the life of the man it commemorates. Sextus Congenius Verus was 42 when he died and had spent 22 years serving aboard the Asclepius. Rather than commemorating a famous emperor or military commander, the monument belonged to an individual whose name and occupation might otherwise have disappeared from the historical record. The inscription preserves details about his age and long career at sea, offering researchers a small but tangible window into the lives of ordinary people within the Roman world. The marble also demonstrates why inscriptions can be so valuable to archaeologists. Even when an artefact becomes separated from its original archaeological context, the information carved into its surface can provide enough evidence to identify both the person it commemorates and the institution that once held it. In this case, those words survived nearly 2,000 years and ultimately helped turn an anonymous garden stone into an identifiable Roman monument.How the Roman tombstone is being returned to ItalyAfter researchers established the stone's connection to the Italian museum, the artefact entered the process of repatriation through cooperation between American and Italian authorities. The FBI's Art Crime Team assisted with the return, with the monument ultimately intended to go back to the institution from which it had disappeared. The return is part of a broader effort by the United States and Italy to recover archaeological and cultural objects that have been removed from their countries of origin. For the Roman funerary monument, however, the journey is unusually personal. The stone travelled from the ancient Roman world to an Italian museum, disappeared from the collection and eventually crossed the Atlantic before spending years in an ordinary New Orleans garden.Where Sextus Congenius Verus's gravestone belongsThe monument is expected to return to the National Archaeological Museum in Civitavecchia, where it can once again be preserved and studied in the country from which it disappeared. For the researchers who identified it, the discovery demonstrates how easily an ancient artefact can become detached from its history. The stone spent years looking like an ordinary piece of marble in a New Orleans garden, while the inscription beneath the surface carried the name of a Roman sailor who lived almost 2,000 years ago. What began with a couple clearing vegetation behind their home ultimately connected archaeologists in Louisiana, Austria and Italy, a missing museum artefact, and a World War II family story. The stone's journey from ancient Rome to Louisiana and, eventually, back toward Italy is now part of the history preserved alongside the monument itself.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2002, Alabama architecture students stacked 72,000 worn carpet tiles into the walls of a family home; Rural Studio has now built more than 200 projects
articles.summary: US News: A house in Alabama contains walls adorned with 72,000 individual stacked tiles held in compression by a heavy wooden-ring beam. Belonging to the Harri.
articles.body: A house in Alabama contains walls adorned with 72,000 individual stacked tiles held in compression by a heavy wooden-ring beam. Belonging to the Harris family, the abode contains a bedroom above and a tornado shelter below. The minds behind the idea trace back to Rural Studio, an off-campus design-build program, rooted in Hale County and part of the School of Architecture, Planning and Landscape Architecture of Auburn University, according to the studio's website.Known as the Lucy Carpet House, it was constructed in 2002 by a team of six students developing a concept assigned by the studio co-founder Sambo Mockbee. The project was a charity house for Lucy and Anderson Harris and their children. It was funded by Interface Carpet. The company donated $30,000, as well as 72,000 pounds of post-consumer carpet tiles. The tiles were held in storage for 7 years to ensure they no longer off-gassed.By creating a system of stacked carpet tiles to make the walls of the house, they were able to conserve enough of the budget to build Lucy the only thing she asked for: a place to pray. For this, Lucy’s bedroom is a sculptural tower, open only to the sky. As she lies in her bed, Lucy can look up at the sky and enjoy the play of light and shadow on the faceted surfaces of her prayer tower.In 1993 two Auburn professors came to this corner of the state, called Hale County, when Newbern was little more than a few dusty streets and churches, and many people were living in precarious old houses. The architects’ proposition was simple: let our students live here and learn by doing, and we will help to build your civic infrastructure. To date, the studio has built more than 200 projects and educated more than 1,200 students in the Black Belt.Around four dozen students are invited to attend each year to participate in this context-based service-learning curriculum, where students live and work alongside our neighbours, finding solutions together. The design-build program challenges students to consider not what can be built but rather what should be built. Their final projects are assessed on whether their structures can stand the test of time, surviving the notorious tornadoes of “Dixie Alley” and the extremes of summer and winter here.“We encourage aspiring young architects to address the ethical responsibility for the social, political, and environmental consequences of what they design and build,” said Andrew Freear, Rural Studio Director.In 2004, Rural Studio began the 20K Initiative to focus students’ efforts on creating single-family detached housing that keeps material and labour costs to an affordable minimum. That program and other research projects have yielded a body of knowledge that illuminates a scalable solution to the problem of housing affordability. The studio’s latest effort, the Front Porch Initiative, is working toward that goal with the help of several partners. Through housing designs refined from the 20K Initiative as well as novel financing mechanisms being developed with partners, Rural Studio aims to fundamentally shift models and practices for affordable housing.It might sound idyllic but Newbern is also at the sharp end of rural life. As in many small, isolated communities in the American South, as well as Italy, Spain and elsewhere, old families are dying out or departing for cities in search of work and opportunity. For generations, there was little civic infrastructure to keep people rooted and local leaders now seek out the services of Rural Studio to arrest their town’s decline.Over a period of 30 years, waves of students have created the vast Lions Park in nearby Greensboro, turned a defunct bank building into Newbern Library, which became the first place in town where high-speed internet was available to the public, and built Newbern’s town hall out of cypress logs.Today, the program runs the Front Porch Initiative, working with housing providers and organisations nationwide to scale their high-performance, affordable rural housing designs into commercial reality.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2009, a Sydney couple moved to a remote Tasmanian island; they stayed for nine years
articles.summary: Rest of World News: John and Bev O’Brien left Sydney in search of a different way of living, and in 2009, that search took them to Three Hummock Island, a remote State Re.
articles.body: John and Bev O’Brien left Sydney in search of a different way of living, and in 2009, that search took them to Three Hummock Island, a remote State Reserve off Tasmania’s north-west coast, where they spent the next nine years managing accommodation and helping care for the island. The couple had no permanent neighbours nearby and lived with the practical limits of an island that could only be reached by small boat, light aircraft or helicopter. They finally left in 2018, and were returning to Sydney after years in a place where some months their Land Rover travelled only about 30 kilometres. According to ABC News, the couple had managed the island’s accommodation business for the entire nine-year period.A job that came with the islandJohn, a former firefighter, and Bev, a teacher, had originally left Sydney to travel and explore other ways of living. They worked as caretakers at the Eyre Bird Observatory in Western Australia, and that was where they heard about the opportunity to manage accommodation on Three Hummock Island.The island was leased by Melbourne businessmen and contained only a few buildings, two airstrips and a jetty. Because it was a Tasmanian State Reserve, the managers had responsibilities beyond looking after guests. When there were visitors, the couple ran the accommodation, and when there were no guests, they worked on the island itself. The couple maintained tracks, painted signs and dealt with the routine jobs required to keep a remote property operating. The island has about 30 kilometres of internal tracks, according to the current Three Hummock Island website.Three Hummock Island covers roughly 7,400 hectares, and its current accommodation operator describes it as extremely remote, with guests required to bring their own food, clothing, medication and other supplies. Electricity comes from renewable sources including wind and solar, while water is supplied by rainwater tanks and a nearby spring.Getting off the island was not simpleWeather was a huge determinant of whether anyone could reach the island or leave it. Three Hummock Island sits in Bass Strait, where strong winds and rough seas can make travel difficult. John installed a weather station and initially set its wind alarm at 55 knots. Storms repeatedly triggered it, so he raised the setting several times. The highest wind speed he recorded was 86 knots, more than 160 kilometres per hour, according to his account to ABC News.About five years before the couple left, John fell from a ladder and broke his back, and it took nine hours for him to reach hospital in Burnie. In 2017, a different emergency unfolded close to their home: the fishing boat Japara caught fire within sight of the couple’s kitchen. The O’Briens helped the crew ashore, gave them showers and clothing, and the men were later taken by helicopter for treatment for smoke inhalation.The wildlife was part of daily lifeForester kangaroos were among the animals the couple saw regularly, along with seabirds and other species. John told ABC that the kangaroos appeared to become accustomed to him and Bev. “A stranger arriving on the island was a different matter”, he said. One night, a little penguin appeared at their door during bad weather. Bev opened it and found the bird standing outside. It was one of the encounters the couple remembered after leaving.Bev recalled a female kangaroo that had become too weak to stand, and another kangaroo remained beside her before she died overnight. The couple also became experienced boaters during their stay. They caught fish for themselves and regularly ate oysters and abalone, and their knowledge of the surrounding waters became part of the practical routine of living so far from the mainland.Nine years later, they went back to SydneyBy April 2018, the O’Briens had decided it was time to leave. They had spent nine years on Three Hummock Island, and family was one of the reasons they wanted to return. The couple told ABC they had not spent Christmas with their relatives for 11 years. During the boat trip away, Bev kept looking back at the island and crying. The following day, the couple could still see its outline from Stanley in northern Tasmania. John was more ready to return to city life, while Bev was still struggling with the departure. Their next plans were less isolated: they were considering a boating trip along the Murray River.Three Hummock Island remains a State Reserve and continues to receive visitors. Its current accommodation is based at the Homestead, a four-bedroom property that can accommodate up to eight people. Visitors still have to arrange transport by air or sea, and the island operates on a pack-in, pack-out basis for rubbish and unused food.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1971, a Canadian art student visited a fogbound island to draw wild horses; she stayed nearly 50 years studying its wildlife, and Sable became a national park reserve
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover the inspiring journey of Zoe Lucas, a Canadian art student who dedicated nearly 50 years to studying and conserving the wildlife of Sable Island, now a national park reserve. Learn about the impact of her work on wild horses, seals, and the island's ecosystem.
articles.body: In 1971, Zoe Lucas arrived on Sable Island as a young art student, drawn by its remote landscape and wild horses. What began as a short visit to the windswept island soon became a lifelong connection. Lucas kept returning, eventually spending more than five decades documenting its horses, wildlife and changing ecosystem through field observation and research.According to Parks Canada, Sable Island lies about 290 kilometres southeast of Halifax, Nova Scotia, and stretches roughly 42 kilometres across the North Atlantic. The island's shifting sand, dunes, freshwater ponds and coastal habitats support wild horses, grey seals and large seabird colonies. More than 350 shipwrecks have also been recorded in its surrounding waters since the 16th century. For Lucas, an early fascination with Sable Island's horses grew into decades of observing and documenting its wider wildlife and changing ecosystem.From sketches to field notebooksLucas did not arrive as a trained biologist. She studied art and goldsmithing, and first visited the island while she was a student. She later became involved with a Dalhousie University seal research programme, an experience that shifted her attention from simply observing the island to documenting its wildlife. By the mid-1980s, she had moved permanently to Sable Island and was spending much of her time there. Her efforts did not just include horses. As years passed, she kept track of seals, conducted beach surveys for birds affected by oil and other forms of marine debris, and documented the occurrence of other organisms. She worked on many flora-and-fauna projects, helping turn the island into a place where long-term changes could be observed.The horses remained central to much of Lucas’s work. She and other researchers built detailed records of individual animals, tracking family relationships, movements, births and deaths. Their observations also helped investigate the long-standing question of the horses’ origins. According to the Journal of Heredity, genetic analysis found no evidence to support the popular theory that Sable Island’s horses descended from shipwrecked Spanish horses. Instead, the horses were found to be more closely related to light draft and multipurpose breeds common in eastern Canada, while remaining genetically distinct as a population.A complicated relationship with the landscapeThe horses are not simply picturesque symbols of wilderness. They are large herbivores living on a narrow island where vegetation, freshwater and dunes are closely connected. Their grazing can therefore influence the plants that help hold parts of the sandy landscape together. According to The Canadian Field-Naturalist, a study involving Zoe Lucas compared vegetation inside and outside fenced areas that excluded horses from grazing. The researchers found that the effects were strongest in marram grassland, where standing plant litter and vegetation cover differed between grazed and ungrazed areas, although plant species richness and diversity were not substantially affected. The findings suggest that the horses influence parts of the island's vegetation, particularly its marram-dominated grasslands.The relationship between the horses and vegetation also needs to be viewed in the context of Sable Island’s constantly changing landscape and fluctuating horse population. Parks Canada records show the number of horses increasing from 138 in 2004 to 591 in 2022, before falling to 374 in 2023 and rising to 420 in 2024. However, Parks Canada cautions that the estimates vary in precision, with most based on annual counts and some on aerial photography. The figures should therefore be interpreted with care rather than seen as a straightforward population trend. On an island shaped by shifting dunes, storms and changing vegetation, grazing is just one of several forces influencing the landscape.From remote refuge to protected landscape Lucas's long association with Sable Island also unfolded alongside growing efforts to protect it. According to Parks Canada, the island was designated a Migratory Bird Sanctuary in 1977 before receiving stronger legal protection decades later. On October 17, 2011, the governments of Canada and Nova Scotia signed an agreement to establish Sable Island as a national park reserve. The final legislative step came on December 1, 2013, when the legislation came into force and formally brought Sable Island National Park Reserve under the Canada National Parks Act, making it Canada's 43rd national park.The designation protects 31 square kilometres of land and its intertidal areas, with ecological integrity at the centre of management. It also reflects the wider value of the island, which supports not only its famous wild horses but also a major breeding colony of grey seals and numerous bird species. In 2024, Lucas was appointed a Member of the Order of Canada in recognition of her decades of work on Sable Island.For more than five decades, Lucas's work has helped turn attention towards an island that might otherwise have remained known mainly for its shipwrecks and wild horses. Her records have provided a long-term view of how its animals, vegetation and shifting landscape change over time. Today, Sable Island remains a place where nature is constantly in motion, and where understanding those changes is as important as protecting the landscape itself.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1951, an English couple moved with four children to roadless Three Hummock Island; they stayed until 2006 as most of its 7,400 hectares became protected
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover the remarkable journey of the Alliston family who lived on Three Hummock Island, Tasmania, for 55 years, shaping its transformation from a pastoral settlement into a protected ecological haven spanning 7,400 hectares.
articles.body: In 1951, an English couple moved with their four children to a remote island in Bass Strait, off north-west Tasmania, to build a life far from mainland routines. John and Eleanor Alliston settled on Three Hummock Island, a roadless landscape where supplies, transport and communication were difficult, and daily life depended heavily on self-reliance. They lived on the island for 55 years, while the surrounding landscape gradually shifted from a working settlement toward formal conservation.According to the history of Three Hummock Island, the island covers about 7,400 hectares and forms part of the Hunter Island Group in western Bass Strait. It takes its name from three prominent hills, the highest rising to about 237 metres. Its landscape includes beaches, lagoons, swamps, woodland and coastal scrub, providing habitat for a variety of birds and other wildlife. Most of the island was declared a nature reserve in 1978, while its protected status was strengthened when it became a State Reserve in 2001.A family life far from the mainlandThe Allistons arrived when Three Hummock Island was still associated with pastoral activity. They took over from the Nichols family, who had previously operated a farm there, and made their home at Chimney Corner. Their four children, Venetia, Robert, Warwick and Ingrid, spent part of their childhood in a place without ordinary roads or urban conveniences. Isolation was part of everyday life. Farming was physically demanding, while supplies and travel to and from the mainland depended on boats or aircraft. Weather could disrupt those connections, making careful planning and a degree of self-sufficiency essential.Eleanor Alliston later recorded the family's experiences in her books Escape to an Island and An Island Affair. Her accounts provide a rare personal perspective on raising children in such a remote environment and adapting to the practical demands of island life. The family's long connection to Three Hummock Island is documented as part of the island's history, with the Allistons spending about 55 years there after arriving in 1951. By the end of that period, the island had undergone a major change in its official status and purpose.A landscape shaped by settlementThree Hummock Island's environmental history is more complex than that of an untouched wilderness. European settlement introduced grazing, clearing and fires that changed sections of the island's vegetation. Scientific surveys have since documented the effects of those changes. According to research published in Papers and Proceedings of the Royal Society of Tasmania, a botanical survey recorded 289 vascular plant species on Three Hummock Island, including 60 introduced species. The researchers also identified six native plants regarded as rare or vulnerable. Much of the island's former Eucalyptus viminalis forest had disappeared, with grazing, fire and other human influences contributing to changes in vegetation. The findings illustrate how even a remote island can carry a long record of human influence. Its ecological character is shaped not only by wind, storms and natural succession but also by decades of farming and land management.From remote settlement to protected landscapeInstead, it placed that history within a landscape increasingly managed for its ecological value. Three Hummock Island became a State Reserve in 2001, strengthening its place within Tasmania's protected-area system. The protected landscape contains a mixture of coastal and inland habitats. Research has shown that its vegetation includes extensive areas of scrub and woodland, while its beaches and wetlands provide habitat for birds and other wildlife. The island has also been recognised as an important breeding area for species including Cape Barren geese and other seabirds.The Allistons did not simply visit a remote wilderness; they lived there through changing seasons, difficult transport and the gradual transformation of the island's official role. During their years on Three Hummock Island, its importance increasingly shifted from a remote pastoral outpost towards a protected natural landscape. Its remoteness, challenging conditions and distinctive habitats became part of the case for protecting the island. For the Allistons, however, Three Hummock Island was first a home. Their move there in 1951 created a way of life few families would have experienced, and more than half a century later, their story remained closely tied to the island's transformation from an isolated settlement into a protected landscape.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Scientists took 232 gravity readings across a Utah mountain and discovered 1.55 million cubic metres of ice hidden beneath loose rock, enough frozen water to fill about 600 Olympic swimming pools
articles.summary: US News: From a distance it looks like nothing more than a sprawling pile of rocks high in Utah’s Wasatch Range. But beneath the rubble of Mount Timpanogos is .
articles.body: From a distance it looks like nothing more than a sprawling pile of rocks high in Utah’s Wasatch Range. But beneath the rubble of Mount Timpanogos is a spectacular hidden reservoir: ice enough to hold some 1.55 million cubic meters of water, which is about 600 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Now, researchers at the University of Utah have mapped this invisible ice using an unusual approach: measuring tiny variations in gravity across the rocky landscape, the university website reports. It’s the Timpanogos Rock Glacier, one of hundreds of rock glaciers in Utah. Unlike normal glaciers, which are large masses of exposed ice and snow, rock glaciers are covered by a thick mantle of loose rock. That rocky exterior is difficult to study, but below it there may be vast amounts of frozen water, the news report states. Timpanogos Rock Glacier is estimated to be around 83% ice and 17% loose rock and is particularly ice-rich. At its deepest point, the ice is buried about 150 feet beneath the surface. According to glaciologist Leif Anderson, “There’s a lot of ice hiding in Utah’s mountains.” Hikers walking over what seems to be normal rubble may be blissfully unaware that dozens of meters of ice could be underneath. Scroll down to read more about it.232 gravity readings have uncovered the secret iceIn fall 2024, University of Utah geologist Bronson Cvijanovich led fieldwork at the glacier to get a better sense of what was beneath the surface. The team made six trips to the site, carrying sensitive scientific equipment up a tough trail. The site is accessible from a trailhead, but it’s a five-mile hike and climb of some 3,500 feet to reach the rock glacier. The researchers used a sophisticated gravimeter to take readings at 232 locations about 25 meters apart. It measures small variations in gravitational acceleration resulting from density differences. Areas with thicker buried ice have a slightly weaker pull from gravity, because rock is much denser than ice. Scientists corrected the measurements for elevation, latitude, terrain, and gravitational effects from the Sun and Moon. They then used Bayesian statistical modeling to generate a three-dimensional picture of the ice under the rocks. It gave an unprecedented view of the interior of Timpanogos Rock Glacier.How does ice get under all that rock?The researchers also explored yet another equally interesting question: how does a rock glacier develop ice when its surface is covered with rocks? The answer seems to be a combination of snowfall and rockfall. Rock glaciers often occur beneath steep mountain slopes and cirques where rocks frequently break loose. Large rocks falling on areas of persistent snow can bury and protect the snow from melting. This process adds ice to the rock glacier over time. Researchers found that years with heavy snowfall, cool summers and substantial rockfalls can contribute to ice accumulation. More than 70 patches of debris-covered snow still exist at Timpanogos, scientists have found.The secret water reserves in a warming climateThe discovery could have implications far beyond Mount Timpanogos. Utah has 836 known rock glaciers, but researchers believe there are about 50,000 rock glaciers worldwide. The authors estimate that the world's rock glaciers contain about 48 gigatons of water by using a correlation between the surface area of a rock glacier and its buried ice volume. Rock glaciers in Utah may contain about one gigaton of water, or about 815,000 acre-feet. Scientists note that not all rock glaciers are necessarily gaining ice today. Some have already lost their frozen hearts. But Timpanogos Rock Glacier seems to still be active, adding ice.Why are rock glaciers important?Such hidden ice reserves could be especially significant to a warm, dry state like Utah. A thick layer of rock helps shield the ice below from heat and sun, potentially allowing rock glaciers to keep water around longer than exposed ice. The research also alters scientists’ view of these formations. Some rock glaciers are not just relics of ancient glacial history but are dynamic systems interacting with today's climate. So what looks from above like a normal field of rocks could be concealing a large reserve of frozen water—and new scientific tools are finally allowing scientists to see what is underneath.Images Courtesy: The University of UtahCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: No surrender, no dissent: How six months of war hardened Iran’s leadership
articles.summary: Middle East News: Six months into its war with the United States and Israel, Iran’s leadership has tightened its grip around a core of hard-line military commanders and.
articles.body: Six months into its war with the United States and Israel, Iran’s leadership has tightened its grip around a core of hard-line military commanders and clerics, signalling that it will resist US pressure abroad while moving aggressively to prevent dissent at home.A series of senior appointments announced on August 11 and 12 has placed veteran Revolutionary Guard figures and security officials at the heart of Iran’s leadership. The moves come as Tehran prepares for a potentially prolonged confrontation with Washington, rejects trust in negotiations with President Donald Trump and faces mounting economic pressure from the US blockade and new sanctions.The appointments have also made clear that Iran’s rulers are preparing for unrest even as no fresh nationwide protests have emerged. The choice of Hossein Taeb, a veteran intelligence chief who has overseen major crackdowns on protests, to lead the Basij volunteer force is being viewed as a particularly strong warning to potential dissenters.Tehran warns of a wider confrontationIran’s new secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, has adopted a defiant tone towards Washington.“If (Trump) wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” Rezaei said last weekend. In a post on X, he warned that “if the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported” from the Persian Gulf.His remarks came as Iran faces the prospect of further US military action. Tehran has little faith in reaching a lasting agreement with Trump after coming under attack twice while negotiations were under way. Iranian officials are also believed to be preparing for another possible assault once Washington replenishes its stocks of missile interceptors.The threat of escalation comes alongside an increasingly severe economic squeeze. The US blockade and planned sanctions risk further damaging an economy already struggling with the impact of the war.Rezaei has nevertheless left the door open to negotiations, but only if Washington changes course. On Monday, he told Pakistani mediator Gen. Asim Munir that the US should “change its attitude and take practical action about implementing the conditions” of the ceasefire deal.Hardliners tighten grip around new supreme leaderRezaei’s appointment was part of a wider reshuffle ordered by Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has been consolidating his leadership after the death of his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.The elder Khamenei, who had led Iran for about 37 years, was killed in US and Israeli strikes launched on February 28. Much of Iran’s senior leadership was also killed in the bombing campaign.The younger Khamenei, 56, has not appeared publicly or been heard in video or audio since the strikes. He is believed to have been wounded. His continued absence could reflect the extraordinary security measures around him, given that he is likely to remain an Israeli target, or the severity of his injuries.His first major appointments suggest that he is relying heavily on a group of longstanding military and security allies.Rezaei, 71, commanded the Revolutionary Guard during much of its formative period, including the 1980-1988 war with Iraq, and remained in the post until 1997. He has also contested Iran’s presidential election several times as a hard-line candidate.Brig. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, 68, has been confirmed as head of the Revolutionary Guard after serving as acting commander since his predecessor was killed alongside the elder Khamenei. Gen. Ali Ozmaei and Gen. Ali Abdollahi have also been confirmed in senior military positions.Sascha Bruchmann, an analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies’ Middle East office in Bahrain, described the appointments as evidence of an effort to maintain unity at the top.“They are a clique of older senior officers who’ve served together over the last decades,” Bruchmann said.“ It looks like internal cohesion, as in hard core people are being pulled into the inner circle,” he said.Taeb appointment sends warning on dissentPerhaps the clearest indication of Tehran’s domestic priorities is the appointment of Taeb as head of the Basij, the Revolutionary Guard’s volunteer street force.The 63-year-old cleric has a long record of suppressing protests. He led the Basij during the mass demonstrations that followed the disputed 2009 re-election of hard-line president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, when dozens of people were killed.Taeb was later appointed head of the Revolutionary Guard’s intelligence organisation, a position he held for nearly 13 years before being removed in 2022. His departure reportedly followed a shake-up prompted by Israeli espionage successes.The Basij operates a nationwide network of volunteers with a presence in streets, government offices and cultural centres. Its role is to reinforce loyalty to Iran’s theocratic system and promote what the leadership describes as ideological purity.Taeb’s return to a frontline security position suggests that Tehran is preparing to confront discontent before it develops into another mass movement.“Putting someone from an intelligence background in charge of the people that would do the crackdown makes sense,” Bruchmann said.The Basij expanded its presence during the war, while hard-liners have staged nightly rallies in Tehran and other cities. The gatherings have sought to demonstrate support for the government and intimidate potential opponents.In his appointment decree, Khamenei ordered Taeb to expand the Basij’s presence in Iranian social life, make greater use of new technologies and “promote the Basij across the world against Zionist-American arrogance”. The wording could also point to a greater role for the force in building links with Iran’s overseas allies and proxies.Taeb has also warned that US economic pressure is designed to divide Iranian society.“If the mosque becomes the center of the neighborhood, the nation will protect its unity, which will be a greater deterrent than any missile.”Economic crisis exposes divisions inside IranThe leadership’s increasingly hard-line posture comes as ordinary Iranians struggle with the economic consequences of the war.There has so far been no clear sign of a new nationwide protest movement, despite growing difficulties in affording basic goods. But the worsening economic situation has exposed differences within the political establishment over how far Iran should continue confronting Washington.President Masoud Pezeshkian remains one of the most prominent voices advocating a negotiated settlement. His allies have argued that Tehran risks weakening itself by prolonging the conflict while its economy deteriorates.“It would be better to bring the war to an end, since today we enjoy power and dignity and the entire world approved our victory, and the U.S. is hated,” Pezeshkian said last week.He has also defended the June ceasefire agreement, rejecting accusations from hard-liners that it gave away too much.The ceasefire quickly collapsed as the US, Israel and Iran resumed exchanges of strikes. Tehran has since demanded the release of billions of dollars in frozen assets under the agreement, along with formal authority over the Strait of Hormuz.Homayoun Falakshahi, the top oil analyst for global commerce information firm Kpler, said the latest appointments pointed to a tougher approach.The selection of Rezaei and Vahidi showed “greater influence for officials associated with a tougher stance,” he wrote.But he cautioned that escalation carries major risks for Tehran. Iran could struggle to “escalate enough to restore deterrence without triggering retaliation that leaves it worse off”.Iran’s leadership faces a choiceThe emerging power structure therefore presents a stark contrast to Trump’s early hopes that the war could help topple Iran’s Islamic Republic and bring more conciliatory figures to power.Instead, six months of conflict have strengthened the influence of officials with decades of experience in Iran’s military and security establishment.Tehran’s leaders appear determined to maintain confrontation with Washington while ensuring that economic hardship does not translate into political unrest.The result is a leadership that is simultaneously preparing for another possible US attack, threatening retaliation and reinforcing the machinery used to suppress domestic opposition.Tehran-based political analyst Ahmad Zeidabadi said there are “serious differences over the future path of the country”.Hard-liners oppose normalisation with the US because “their survival depends on the existence of conflict and hostility,” he wrote in the newspaper Hammihan, which supports Pezeshkian.For now, the balance of power appears to favour those advocating resistance rather than compromise. Iran’s new leadership is signalling that it will not easily yield to US demands abroad, while showing that dissent at home will face an equally uncompromising response.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russian strikes kill at least one in Odessa, cause blast near Kiev
articles.summary: At least one person has been killed and three others wounded following overnight Russian strikes on the Odessa region in southern Ukraine, the region's gover...
articles.body:
At least one person has been killed and three others wounded following overnight Russian strikes on the Odessa region in southern Ukraine, the region's governor said on Saturday.

Oleh Kiper said on Telegram that five grain transporters had been burned out and three others damaged. All fires were extinguished, he said.

Earlier, the administration of the Izmail district, where the country's Danube ports are located, had warned of Russian drones in the area. Transport infrastructure facilities were damaged, it said.

Several people were also killed on Friday evening near the village of Myla, around 5 kilometres west of the capital Kiev, after a fire triggered by explosions.

"We do not yet have sufficient information on the number of casualties," Kiev Governor Tymur Tkachenko wrote on Telegram.

The prosecutor's office opened an investigation into "negligence in the line of duty" and initially reported five people wounded following a possible drone strike. Russia said an ammunition depot was the target of the attack.

The main road connecting Kiev to the west had to be completely closed over a stretch of several kilometres to allow firefighting and rescue operations to take place. Videos on social media showed fire and explosions in the evening twilight.

Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi pointed to a similar incident in early July on the south-western outskirts of Kiev. "In the fifth year of the war, the same mistakes are being made: This is criminal negligence," he wrote on Telegram.

At least two people were also wounded in Kiev itself, according to authorities. Ukraine has been defending itself against the Russian invasion for more than four and a half years.

Seven injured as Ukrainian drones hit Russia's Rostov region

Meanwhile, at least seven people have been wounded in a wave of Ukrainian airstrikes on the Rostov region in southern Russia, local authorities said on Saturday.

Two children were taken to hospital, one with very serious injuries, state news agency TASS reported, citing Governor Yuri Slyusar. Two residential blocks in the port city of Rostov-on-Don were damaged by falling drone debris, according to the report.

Ukrainian media reported that a warehouse belonging to an electronics retailer also caught fire.

The reports could not be independently verified.

For weeks, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly targeted the logistics centres of major Russian companies. Online retailers Wildberries and Ozon have been among the main targets.

The strikes have caused damage running into the billions and have brought renewed attention to the consequences of Russia's war on its neighbour. Kiev's leadership is also seeking to influence the political mood in Russia ahead of parliamentary elections scheduled for September 18 to 20.

Ukraine has been defending itself against Russia's destructive war for four and a half years with the help of Western military aid. Both sides deploy vast numbers of drones in their mutual strikes, as the weapons are relatively cheap to produce and difficult to intercept when deployed in large numbers.

During some attack waves, hundreds of drones are used simultaneously to overwhelm air defences. Both sides accuse each other of deliberately targeting civilians, though casualties and damage on the Ukrainian side are far greater.
